title: Affine root scheme represents roots on all test schemes
statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $n\geq1$, $V=\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], and $P=\operatorname{Spec}(R[t]/(t^n-1))$, using polynomial rings [def-weil-polynomial-ring] and quotient algebras [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. Write $x\in\Gamma(P,\mathcal O_P)$ for the class of $t$; it is a unit with inverse $x^{n-1}$. For every $V$-scheme $U$ [def-pc-scheme], pullback of $x$ gives a bijection
$$\operatorname{Mor}_V(U,P)\xrightarrow{\sim}\{z\in\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)^\times:z^n=1\},\qquad a\longmapsto a^\sharp(x),$$
natural in all morphisms of $V$-schemes $U$. In particular this identifies the representable sheaf $h_P$, $h_P(W)=\operatorname{Mor}_V(W,P)$ [lem-weil-pbc-small-etale-representable-presheaf-sheaf], on the small etale site [def-weil-pbc-etale-site] with the underlying sheaf of sets of the roots sheaf [def-asd-etale-roots-of-unity]. For every morphism of schemes $v:V'\to V$ and $P'=V'\times_VP$ [def-pc-fibre-product], with projection $p:P'\to P$, the same formula $a\mapsto a^\sharp(p^\sharp x)$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Mor}_{V'}(U,P')$ to these roots for every $V'$-scheme $U$, natural in $U$. Under these bijections base-changing $a:U\to P$ sends its root to the pullback of that root along $V'\times_VU\to U$.

proof.text: Put $B=R[t]/(t^n-1)$ and let $q:R[t]\to B$ be the quotient map. Its kernel is $(t^n-1)$, so $q(t)^n=1$. Under $B=\Gamma(P,\mathcal O_P)$ this says $x^n=1$. Since $n\geq1$, $xx^{n-1}=x^{n-1}x=x^n=1$, so $x$ has the asserted inverse. Give $P$ its $V$-structure by the spectrum of the composite $R\to R[t]\xrightarrow q B$.

source.place: Tag 040M, example-roots-of-unity: the affine presentation and its universal coordinate

proof.text: Fix any structure morphism $s:U\to V$, put $C=\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)$ and write $\rho:R\to C$ for $s^\sharp$. The affine-target morphism lemma, applied to $B$ and to $R$, gives bijections between morphisms $U\to P$ and ring maps $\varphi:B\to C$, and between morphisms $U\to V$ and ring maps $R\to C$. By the definition of composition of scheme morphisms, the composite $U\to P\to V$ induces $\varphi\circ(R\to B)$. Thus it equals $s$ exactly when $\varphi$ is an $R$-algebra homomorphism. This restricts the first bijection to $\operatorname{Mor}_V(U,P)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{R\text{-alg}}(B,C)$. No affineness assumption on $U$ has been made.

source.place: Tag 01I1, lemma-morphism-into-affine; applied to the presentation of Tag 040M

proof.text: For $c\in C$ define $E_c:R[t]\to C$ by $E_c(\sum_i r_it^i)=\sum_i\rho(r_i)c^i$. These are finite sums. This preserves addition and $1$, and the convolution formula for multiplication gives $E_c(fg)=\sum_{i,j}\rho(r_i)\rho(s_j)c^{i+j}=E_c(f)E_c(g)$. It extends $\rho$ and sends $t$ to $c$. Conversely any ring map extending $\rho$ with $t\mapsto c$ must have this formula, because each polynomial is the finite sum of its coefficient monomials. Hence it is the unique such map.

source.place: Tag 040M, example-roots-of-unity: elementary evaluation calculation for the displayed polynomial ring

proof.text: If $c^n=1$, then $E_c(t^n-1)=0$, and $\varphi_c(q(f))=E_c(f)$ is well defined: when $q(f)=q(g)$ the difference $f-g$ lies in $(t^n-1)$, so it is $(t^n-1)h$ for a polynomial $h$, and its evaluation is zero. The quotient map is surjective, so this formula defines an $R$-algebra map and determines it uniquely. Conversely any $\varphi:B\to C$ gives $c=\varphi(q(t))$ with $c^n=1$, and $\varphi q=E_c$ by step 3, so $\varphi=\varphi_c$. Thus steps 2--4 give exactly $a\mapsto a^\sharp(x)$ as a bijection with $\{c\in C:c^n=1\}$. Every such $c$ is a unit with inverse $c^{n-1}$, and a unit is determined by its underlying element; consequently this is the required bijection with the roots in $C^\times$.

source.place: Tag 040M, example-roots-of-unity: elementary quotient and inverse calculations establishing its functor of points

proof.text: For any morphism $b:U_1\to U_2$ over $V$ and any $a:U_2\to P$, the definition of composition gives $(a\circ b)^\sharp(x)=b^\sharp(a^\sharp(x))$. A ring homomorphism takes a unit with inverse $y$ to a unit with inverse the image of $y$, and preserves $n$-th powers. Thus this is equality of the roots on both sides, proving naturality in every morphism of $V$-schemes.

source.place: Tag 040M, example-roots-of-unity: functor of points, naturality by composition

proof.text: Restrict the bijections to the objects $U\to V$ of the small etale site. The representable-presheaf sheaf lemma applies to the $V$-scheme $P$ and shows that $U\mapsto\operatorname{Mor}_V(U,P)$ is a sheaf of sets. The roots-of-unity definition assigns to each such $U$ exactly $\{z\in\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)^\times:z^n=1\}$, and its restrictions are pullback on sections. Step 5 shows that the bijections commute with these restrictions, so their inverses do as well. They therefore identify $h_P$ with the underlying sheaf of sets of $\mu_{n,V}$. The lemma does not require $P\to V$ to be etale.

source.place: Tag 03PK, section-kummer, first paragraph, using Tag 03O3, lemma-representable-sheaf-fpqc

proof.text: Let $v:V\prime\to V$ be arbitrary, let $P\prime=V\prime\times_V P$, and write $p:P\prime\to P$ and $\pi:P\prime\to V\prime$ for its projections. For a $V\prime$-scheme $s:U\to V\prime$, the fibre-product universal property makes $a\mapsto p\circ a$ a bijection $\operatorname{Mor}_{V\prime}(U,P\prime)\to\operatorname{Mor}_V(U,P)$, where $U$ is given the $V$-structure $v\circ s$: its inverse sends $b$ to the unique pair $(s,b)$. The projection equations prove that these maps are inverse and commute with precomposition. Composing with steps 2--5 gives the desired natural bijection, and its value is $(p\circ a)^\sharp(x)=a^\sharp(p^\sharp x)$. This does not require $V\prime$ to be affine.

source.place: Tag 040M, example-roots-of-unity: base-change paragraph, expanded by the fibre-product universal property

proof.text: Finally let $a:U\to P$ be over $V$, put $U\prime=V\prime\times_V U$ with projection $r:U\prime\to U$, and let $a\prime:U\prime\to P\prime$ be its base change. The defining projection equation is $p\circ a\prime=a\circ r$. Applying the maps on sections to $x$ gives $(a\prime)^\sharp(p^\sharp x)=r^\sharp(a^\sharp x)$. This identifies the root of the base-changed morphism with the pullback of the original root, exactly as asserted.
